claims.text: Nanoparticle stability under catalytic and thermoelectric service conditions is governed by a temperature-activated balance between surface or near-surface diffusion and bulk atomic ordering.
Below a critical temperature, limited atomic mobility preserves homogeneous elemental mixing.
Above a critical temperature, increased diffusion facilitates local compositional fluctuations and segregation at surfaces and interfaces.
Surface or interfacial segregation can destabilize nanoparticle structure and chemical uniformity.
The proposed initial state consists of near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles with a homogeneous elemental distribution.
Stepwise in situ vacuum annealing in an aberration-corrected STEM is proposed as the controlled intervention.
Local segregation patterns at surfaces and interfaces are mediated by temperature-dependent diffusion kinetics.
Crossing the critical annealing temperature causes increased surface diffusion that triggers local segregation or interfacial reordering.
Local segregation or interfacial reordering leads to structural instability.
Temperature-induced segregation or reordering may change catalytic or thermoelectric performance.
Nanoparticles annealed below the critical threshold will retain an atomic distribution similar to the homogeneous baseline.
Nanoparticles annealed above the critical threshold will develop measurable compositional heterogeneity.
Changes in STEM contrast or EDS maps can reveal the predicted compositional heterogeneity.
The predicted compositional heterogeneity would be indicative of phase separation or clustering.
The proposed relationship is limited to initially uniform, near-equiatomic nanoparticles under high-vacuum annealing.
Chemical species in the environment or particle supports may alter the observed behavior.
The critical temperature and extent of segregation depend on elemental diffusion coefficients and bonding energetics.
